The central question is whether KV cache eviction policies — which decide which token representations to discard when the cache fills — should be sensitive to how diffusely or sharply a token is attended to, measured via attention entropy, rather than relying on cruder proxies like recency or cumulative attention score. In long-context retrieval tasks (e.g., needle-in-a-haystack, multi-hop QA over 100k+ tokens), the failure mode is evicting tokens that carry sparse but irretrievable information: a key entity mentioned once, attended to sharply but briefly, then never seen again — a pattern that looks unimportant to recency-based evictors but is catastrophically important to retrieval accuracy. The key concepts are: attention entropy per token per layer (low entropy = a head is selectively attending to that token; high entropy = diffuse, possibly uninformative attention), eviction budget (how many KV pairs you can afford to keep given memory constraints), and the distinction between prefill-time importance estimation versus decode-time dynamic re-weighting, since most eviction decisions must be made before you know which tokens the future query will need. The expert worry that a beginner completely misses is layer heterogeneity: different layers use attention for structurally different purposes (early layers do syntactic/positional work, middle layers aggregate semantics, late layers do task-specific retrieval), so a low-entropy score in layer 2 means something entirely different from a low-entropy score in layer 22 — naive entropy aggregation across layers will actively mislead an eviction policy. A further expert concern is that entropy patterns are query-dependent: the same cached context produces radically different attention distributions depending on what's being decoded, meaning static importance scores computed at prefill time may be systematically wrong for retrieval-heavy decode phases.

The most grounded prefill-time signal is cross-layer attention sink stability: tokens that consistently receive non-trivial attention mass across many layers and many heads — not just as global "sink" tokens like [BOS] — tend to be structurally important regardless of future query content. SnapKV (2024) operationalizes a version of this by observing attention patterns over a prompt window appended to the context (the question prefix itself), using that small attended region to vote on which KV positions to retain; this is query-aware at prefill but reveals the core insight that even a weak query signal dramatically sharpens importance estimation. A genuinely query-agnostic signal that holds up empirically is token positional rarity combined with lexical salience: named entities, numbers, and low-frequency tokens in unusual syntactic positions (subject of a relative clause, appositive NP) receive sharp, low-entropy attention from semantic heads in middle layers during prefill even with no query present, because the model is performing coreference and entity-linking regardless. PyramidKV (2024) exploits the complementary structural insight — that lower layers need more KV budget than higher layers because they carry broader contextual signals — allocating cache non-uniformly across layers based on prefill attention variance, achieving near-lossless retrieval at 20% cache size on RULER benchmarks. The honest expert caveat is that all of these are correlated proxies, not causal ones: a token can be attended to sharply at prefill because it's syntactically prominent, not because it's the retrieval target, and the correlation breaks badly in adversarial or out-of-distribution documents where the critical fact is buried in a syntactically mundane clause.

Once a KV entry is evicted and the original token's activation is not retained, exact recomputation requires a full forward pass over the evicted positions — which costs O(n·d) per layer and is only tractable if you've kept the raw token IDs and positional embeddings in cheap CPU memory, a design choice systems like InfLLM and Memorizing Transformers make explicitly, offloading evicted KV blocks to CPU/disk and retrieving them via approximate nearest-neighbor search on query vectors at decode time. The ANN retrieval path is the key tractability lever: rather than recomputing all evicted tokens, you issue a query vector (the current decode hidden state) against an index of evicted key vectors, retrieve the top-k most relevant, recompute only those KV values, and inject them — InfLLM reports this adds ~15-30% latency overhead versus a full-cache baseline on 100k-token tasks, which is painful but not prohibitive for agentic workloads where latency budgets are looser. The deeper design tension is between eviction granularity and retrievability: if you evict at the individual token level, your ANN index is huge and retrieval is precise; if you evict at the chunk level (e.g., 16- or 32-token windows, as InfLLM does), the index is manageable but you pay for entire chunks even when only one token in the chunk was needed, wasting memory bandwidth. For truly incremental query arrival — where intent reveals itself word by word — the honest answer is that no current system handles this well; the closest approximation is speculative retention, where the policy maintains a "suspicion buffer" of recently evicted blocks that haven't been flushed to slow storage yet, giving a short grace window (perhaps 512–1024 new tokens of decode) during which retrieval is cheap before cold eviction becomes permanent. The fundamental irony is that entropy-based eviction policies are most aggressive on syntactically plain tokens — exactly the tokens most likely to be retrieval targets in needle-in-haystack tasks — meaning entropy-sensitivity without a retrieval fallback actively makes the eviction-then-recover problem harder, not easier.

The severity of the problem is encoding-scheme-dependent: with RoPE (used in LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma, and most production models), position is injected by rotating key and query vectors in 2D subspaces at each layer, which means a token at position 512 and the same token at position 50,000 produce key vectors that are rotated by very different angles — their dot product decays roughly as cos(Δθ·m) where m is the frequency and Δθ is the position gap, so ANN retrieval using cosine similarity will systematically fail to match semantically identical content at distant positions. Empirically, this isn't hypothetical: LongRoPE and YaRN were developed precisely because naive RoPE extrapolation causes attention scores to become noisy and retrieval to degrade past the training context length, with perplexity spikes appearing as early as 2× the training window in unmodified models. One partial mitigation used in retrieval-augmented KV systems is to strip or normalize positional components before indexing: you store the pre-rotation key vector (or a position-agnostic semantic projection) in the ANN index, then re-apply the correct positional rotation after retrieval when computing the actual attention score — this is architecturally clean but requires modifying the KV cache write path and isn't standard in any shipping system as of early 2025. The multi-document case is nastier than single-document long-context because position assignment across documents is arbitrary: if you concatenate three documents at positions 0–10k, 10k–20k, and 20k–30k, the same entity name in document 1 and document 3 gets key vectors that differ purely due to position offset, not semantics, making cross-document ANN retrieval unreliable even within a comfortable RoPE range. The expert punchline is that this reveals a representational conflict at the heart of KV caching: the key vectors that make attention work well (position-sensitive, causally structured) are precisely the wrong vectors to use as semantic retrieval indices, and any system that tries to do both with the same vector is making an architectural compromise that will show up as retrieval failures on multi-document benchmarks like MDQA or HELMET.

The most principled existing approach is low-rank factorization of the key matrix: rather than storing a full second key vector, you store a small projection (e.g., 64 or 128 dimensions versus the full 128-per-head in LLaMA-3) of the pre-rotation key as a retrieval index, accepting that the index is lossy but betting that semantic identity survives low-rank compression better than positional displacement does — this is essentially what MagicPIG (2024) does, using LSH on compressed key representations to identify candidate tokens before full attention recomputation, reporting 90%+ recall on retrieval tasks at ~20% of the index footprint cost. A complementary structural insight comes from multi-head latent attention (MLA) in DeepSeek-V2: the architecture explicitly decomposes the KV representation into a low-rank latent vector (which is position-agnostic and cheap to store) plus a position-sensitive component injected only at attention-compute time, achieving a 93% KV cache size reduction versus standard MHA while preserving attention quality — this is the closest shipping system to "two keys for free," because the latent vector is the semantic retrieval index and the positional component is computed on-the-fly rather than cached. The catch with MLA-style designs is that they require architectural commitment at training time: you can't retrofit a latent decomposition onto a RoPE-trained LLaMA model without retraining, so this path is unavailable for eviction policies applied to existing deployed models. For post-hoc systems without architectural changes, the least bad option is hierarchical indexing: maintain a coarse semantic cluster index (k-means over position-stripped key vectors, computed once at prefill) that narrows the candidate set to ~1% of tokens, then do exact positional-key attention over only those candidates — this avoids the footprint doubling at the cost of a clustering pass and imperfect recall at cluster boundaries. The deeper principle is that the tension dissolves if you accept asymmetric key roles by layer: early layers where positional structure dominates can use recency-based eviction without a retrieval index at all, while middle layers where semantic heads concentrate can carry the dual-representation overhead only where it buys something — a layer-adaptive policy that no current system fully implements but that the PyramidKV / SnapKV literature is converging toward implicitly.

This is a real and underappreciated failure mode: MLA's shared latent vector of dimension d_c (512 in DeepSeek-V2 versus 128×128=16,384 total head-key capacity in equivalent MHA) must simultaneously encode signals for all heads via learned up-projection matrices W_UK, which means the latent is optimized for the average reconstruction loss across heads — minority heads tracking rare syntactic or coreference features will have their signals systematically down-weighted if those features are low-frequency in the training distribution. The evidence that head specialization is real and uneven is well-established: Clark et al. (2019) on BERT showed that specific heads handle specific relations (e.g., head 8-10 tracks direct objects, head 5-4 tracks coreferents) with near-deterministic behavior, and Olsson et al. (2022) demonstrated that induction heads — critical for in-context retrieval — are sparse, sometimes appearing in only 1-2 heads per layer, making them exactly the minority signal a shared bottleneck would compress away. DeepSeek-V2's own ablations show that increasing d_c from 512 to 1024 yields measurable perplexity improvements on long-context benchmarks but diminishing returns on standard evals, which is consistent with the bottleneck selectively hurting rare-retrieval tasks where minority head signals matter most — though the paper doesn't frame it this way explicitly. A concrete failure scenario: in multi-hop reasoning over a long document, an induction head needs to bind "the scientist mentioned in paragraph 3" to a pronoun 40k tokens later; if the latent bottleneck suppresses that head's key signal below the ANN retrieval threshold, the eviction policy discards the paragraph-3 KV block, and the hop silently fails with no recoverable error signal. The mitigation that falls naturally out of this analysis is per-head importance weighting in the up-projection: train W_UK with a sparsity-aware loss that penalizes suppression of heads with high task-specific activation variance, effectively reserving latent capacity for high-entropy minority heads — but no published system does this yet, and it would require knowing which heads are "minority" in a task-adaptive way rather than globally.

The selective exemption idea is sound in principle and has a weak empirical precedent in H2O (Heavy-Hitter Oracle, 2023), which identifies "heavy hitter" tokens per head based on cumulative attention mass and exempts them from eviction — but H2O is head-agnostic, treating all heads equally, so the refinement you're describing is to weight the exemption budget toward heads that behave like induction heads, which would require runtime head classification. Identifying induction heads without full mechanistic analysis is tractable via a prefix-copying diagnostic: feed the model a sequence of the form [A][B]...[A] and measure, for each head, whether attention from the second [A] position spikes onto [B] — induction heads by definition do this, and you can run this probe across a small batch of synthetic sequences in a single forward pass, producing a per-head "induction score" cheaply; Olsson et al. used exactly this method and found induction heads cluster reliably in early-to-middle layers with scores that are bimodal (heads either are or aren't induction heads, with little ambiguity). In practice for a new model you'd run ~100 random prefix-copying sequences, compute mean attention from second-occurrence tokens to their expected continuation positions per head, threshold at say 0.3 normalized attention mass, and get a stable induction head map in under a minute of compute — this is a one-time characterization cost per model that could ship as part of model metadata. The runtime eviction policy then becomes: for each token position, compute a weighted attention score that upweights attention received from identified induction heads by a factor λ (empirically, λ≈3-5 seems reasonable based on the relative rarity of induction heads), and use this reweighted score as the retention priority, exempting top-k tokens per induction head from eviction regardless of their cumulative attention rank globally. The expert concern is induction head interference with entropy-based signals: induction heads produce characteristically low-entropy attention (sharp spikes onto specific prior tokens), which means a naive entropy-based eviction policy already partially protects their targets — but only at the layer where the induction head fires, not in surrounding layers where the same token may look unremarkable, so cross-layer aggregation without head-type awareness will still under-protect induction targets in the layers that matter least mechanistically while over-protecting them in layers where the signal is noise.

The mechanistic answer is that fuzzy induction is handled by query-key similarity in semantic embedding space rather than token-identity matching, and the circuit responsible isn't a single head but a composition: a earlier head constructs a "semantic pointer" (an abstract representation of the query concept) that gets routed via residual stream to a later head which then attends broadly over positions where that concept was instantiated — this is the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit generalized, and Anthropic's Interpretability team's superposition work suggests these composed circuits are common but harder to isolate than pure induction heads because their attention patterns are diffuse rather than spiky. The entropy signature is diagnostically distinct from lexical induction: where induction heads produce near-zero entropy (one sharp spike), fuzzy induction heads produce characteristically medium entropy — attending to a cluster of 5-20 semantically related positions rather than one exact match — which is the worst case for naive entropy-based eviction because medium-entropy attention looks like "noise" or "diffuse uninformative attention" to a policy that treats low entropy as the importance signal, yet it's actually highly structured semantic retrieval. Zaheer et al.'s BigBird (2020) and subsequent sparse attention analyses found that semantic similarity retrieval produces attention patterns with entropy in the 2.5-4.0 nats range (versus <0.5 nats for induction heads and >5 nats for pure sink attention), suggesting there is a detectable entropy band that could serve as a "fuzzy retrieval" signature if you bin entropy rather than threshold it. The eviction policy implication is to treat entropy as a categorical rather than ordinal signal: rather than "lower entropy = more important," you'd maintain separate retention budgets for the low-entropy band (lexical induction targets), the medium-entropy band (fuzzy retrieval targets), and the high-entropy band (contextual/sink tokens worth evicting), with the medium band being the most underprotected by all current systems. The hard unsolved problem is that medium-entropy patterns are also produced by genuinely uninformative diffuse attention — a head that hasn't found anything useful and is spreading mass evenly — and distinguishing "semantically clustered medium entropy" from "confused diffuse medium entropy" requires either a secondary signal (e.g., whether the attended positions share a semantic cluster) or a learned classifier, neither of which operates cheaply enough for an inline eviction policy at current hardware budgets.
